title: How the Nasdaq Foundation is Supporting Rural Founders to Build with AI
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: This spring, a cohort of rural founders set to work learning and experimenting how to apply artificial intelligence to their entrepreneurial ideas, supported by Nasdaq.
content: This spring, a cohort of rural founders set to work learning and experimenting how to apply artificial intelligence to their entrepreneurial ideas. They convened at the Center on Rural Innovation’s AI Forward Studio , a unique hands-on program funded by the Nasdaq Foundation. The program combined learning with weekly check-ins, mentorship, and a peer community – meeting every founder where they were, whether they had never written a line of code or were ready to push past no-code tools entirely. “With Nasdaq Foundation’s support, the Center on Rural Innovation launched AI Forward Studio, a free, 12-week hands-on learning program that brought together 22 rural startups, which included the founders and their teams,” said Diego Rubio, Senior Program Manager for Entrepreneurship Ecosystems at the Center on Rural Innovation. “This unique program gave entrepreneurs the space and support to experiment with AI tools, access technical guidance and mentorship, and connect with peers while applying AI directly to their startups.” The AI Forward Studio was designed to turn that learning into tangible outcomes, Rubio explained, including reaching more customers, securing funding, and building valuable connections. For the Nasdaq Foundation, the program instantly made sense to fund. “When the Center on Rural Innovation applied for a grant from the Nasdaq Foundation to hold their AI Forward Studio, we immediately recognized what a great idea it was,” said Jailan Griffiths, President of the Nasdaq Foundation and Head of Purpose at Nasdaq. “AI is integral to Nasdaq’s strategy and is quickly shaping tomorrow's economy – so a program that combines that with building the future of rural businesses was a really attractive proposal and ticked so many boxes for us when it came our way.” Griffiths pointed to recent research from the Nasdaq Economic Institute that found AI is enabling more entrepreneurship because of decreased financial barriers to building out the initial products and operations of a company. “The AI economy is taking shape in real time, and it is changing who can start a business, how fast can they scale, and what do they need to get started; and the AI Forward Studio makes sure that rural founders are playing a part in that reshaping,” she said. “The founders who get access to the AI tools letting them do more with less are the ones who are going to help author what comes next, and that offers a unique opportunity to support and revitalize rural economies.” Griffiths explained that the foundation, through its Economic Opportunity Grant Program, targets five areas of impact: Empowering individuals through financial literacy Supporting both new and established ventures by improving access to capital Building a new generation shaping the financial markets by cultivating investor identity Enabling employee and community ownership Strengthening economies and opportunities through regional revitalization and rural wealth building Each of those interconnected pillars, she said, ultimately comes back to Nasdaq’s purpose as an organization. “Our purpose is to empower economic opportunity, and that flows through everything that Nasdaq does as an organization – from our business strategy to our product development, the way we engage our clients, and how we run our markets,” Griffiths said. “And it also flows straight through to the Nasdaq Foundation as well – and our grant program explicitly aims to expand access and create opportunity throughout the economy.” The AI Forward Studio, she noted, fit squarely into the “access to capital” and “regional revitalization and rural wealth building” categories by preparing rural businesses for investment readiness. In fact, Griffiths said, many of the founders who participated in the program are not only driven by the goal of growing their own businesses, but also see rural entrepreneurship as an opportunity to help bring their communities along in their success – not just through job creation, but also through sharing skills that will ready the workforce for the future. For the founders participating in the program, the studio also offered a unique opportunity to rapidly move their business ideas forward. "One thing that's been especially valuable about AI Forward Studio has been the speed to which we can iterate and bring forward our software ideas to a viable alpha stage ready for investor review,” said Jason Vanest, the founder of Brattleboro, Vermont-based Logic Building Systems. Van Nest joined the studio with a software concept in mind, and his team successfully built an initial working prototype within days. Similar experiences occurred throughout the studio’s different entrepreneurial endeavors. “Our biggest takeaway from this program was that rural founders are eager to use AI and can move quickly when they have the right tools, guidance, and space to experiment,” Rubio said. “We saw founders turn ideas into working prototypes, build minimum viable products, win funding, and approach investors with real results.” He added that AI tools will clearly continue to evolve, but “the most valuable outcome was giving founders the confidence, fluency, and judgment to keep experimenting, adapting, and creating long after the program ends.”

title: Biweekly Investment Insights: When hawks fly, stay grounded in the fundamentals
author: Yanni Angelakos
description: Markets have turned more cautious following a hawkish Fed message, rising Treasury yields, and trade tensions. While higher rates may pressure equities near term, earnings expectations remain the stronger driver of Nasdaq-100 performance.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Macro & micro square off (again) as investors move past Q2 earnings season Fed Chair Warsh delivered a hawkish speech at Jackson Hole focused on battling inflation Despite government intervention, Treasury yields have rerated higher U.S. corporate earnings strength & credit spreads still point to a constructive backdrop Biweekly Charts in Focus: Rising Treasury yields can dampen market sentiment, but next 12-month consensus EPS have a stronger historical relationship with equity index returns Source: Bloomberg. As of August 31, 2026, monthly basis. Source: Bloomberg. As of August 31, 2026, monthly basis. Summary The end of a strong Q2 earnings season coincided with August NFPs that were notably above estimates and a decisively hawkish message from Federal Reserve Chair Warsh at the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium on August 28 th : “Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do. That’s our job.” After the recent downshift in the market pricing of Fed rate hike expectations through 2026, they have reset higher as have Treasury yields. Higher Treasury yields typically impact equities via a higher risk-free rate which can reduce the present value of future cash flows and compress equity valuations, all else being equal. They can also tighten financial conditions which dampens risk appetite. However, per our Biweekly Charts in Focus, over the past 20 years, annual changes in Treasury 10-year yields cannot effectively predict YoY changes to the Nasdaq-100. It is the fundamentals such as earnings expectations—measured here by the annual change in Nasdaq-100 NTM consensus EPS—which historically have had greater explanatory power in terms of equity index returns. The markets and the economy have lived with higher rates in the past, and the Treasury 10-year yield matches up directionally with U.S. nominal GDP growth since 1980. As we’ve discussed before , it is not just the rise in rates but it is also why rates are rising which is important. Our decomposition model of nominal Treasury 10-year yield changes YTD continues to point to it being overwhelmingly driven by the change in real rates as a byproduct of Fed policy repricing amidst a resilient U.S. economy. Against this backdrop and amidst shifting equity market returns, corporate earnings and revenue estimates remain solid over the next few quarters. But we are watching to see if lower expectations develop into mid-2027. The strong corporate earnings construct is also reflected in U.S. corporate credit spreads which are hovering near 20-year tights. In the very near-term, as the markets push into what has historically been the weakest month for U.S. equity returns (September), equities could remain unsettled amidst the higher rates backdrop, AI capex questions, and ahead of key macro data points that will further inform the September 16 th Fed meeting. Details Hawkish Warsh commentary & higher Treasury yields Fed Chair Warsh’s speech at Jackson Hole was more in-line with the recent tilt of the FOMC in terms of looking to combat inflation sooner than later. Despite better-than-expected PCE and CPI readings recently, he stressed that “they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.” He also noted that “on balance, I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive.” Warsh’s latest comments and stronger August NFPs of 162,000 (above consensus of 55,000), along with the two prior months revised higher by a net of 55,000 jobs, sent another reverberation through the market pricing of Fed rate hike expectations. We admit that we show Figure 3 frequently. While it speaks to the evolving market narrative, it is also a reminder that it is important for investors to remain strategically disciplined, and to focus on the health of corporate fundamentals as well as the structural growth stories amidst the macro volatility [ 1 ] . The combination of a broadly resilient U.S. economy, sticky inflation trends and resurgent energy prices, ongoing U.S. fiscal concerns, the market navigating an evolving Fed communications strategy, and the battle for capital globally between governments and AI-related corporate debt (Goldman Sachs estimates nearly $500 billion of AI-related corporate debt issuance in 2026 YTD), has pushed the long-end of the yield curve higher. Figure 3: Number of 25bp hikes priced in by Fed meeting has round-tripped last 3 weeks Source: Bloomberg Treasury Secretary Bessent announced the long-end liquidity buyback program will at least double, raising the per-operation cap from $2 billion to at least $4 billion for 10-, 20-, and 30-year debt effective September 9 th , with the Treasury General Account potentially tapped to fund the operations rather than issuing additional front-end bills. However, 10-year yields are now higher by more than 10 basis points from when Secretary Bessent announced these measures on August 19 th . So, is the Treasury 10-year yield at its highest since January 2025 out of sync with the fundamentals? With nominal U.S. GDP running at 6.6% YoY, as Figure 4 shows, a 10-year yield of around 4.75% does not seem out of bounds (all else being equal given the various dynamics at play such as term premium, inflation dynamics, etc.). A lender extending 10-year credit to the U.S. government would expect, at minimum, to be compensated for the opportunity cost of capital—which is roughly what the economy can generate in nominal terms. Figure 4: Treasury 10-year yields track directionally with U.S. nominal GDP Source: Bloomberg Shifting equity returns & flows Taking a step back, while macro clouds have gathered (again), we continue to note the broadening of equity returns beneath the index levels. As a proxy for the growth versus value trade, as well as for AI enablers versus AI adopters, Figure 5 shows the massive outperformance of semis relative to banks on a 6-month rolling basis—a +4.1 standard deviation move versus the 10-year average as of mid-June 2026. However, banks recovered on a relative basis on the back of strong earnings and a broadly resilient U.S. economy while semis sold off notably in July (SOX was -20.6%, its largest monthly decline since December 2002). This reversal in sentiment can also be seen through the lens of retail flows across baskets of semiconductor and bank names via Nasdaq Data Link’s U.S. Retail Equities Flow (UREF) dataset. Figure 6 shows the difference in retail buying of semi and bank stocks. Based on UREF data, retail investors began to favor semis relative to banks beginning in December 2023, with this net buying activity peaking in May 2025. Semi retail net buying activity continued to be net positive until July 2026 after which it has turned net negative amidst the sell-off in semis—further illustrating the shift in sentiment and speaking to the recent market rotation. Figure 5: Reversal in semis vs. banks speaks to the broadening of equity returns Figure 6: Mirrored reversal in semi vs. bank net dollar retail flows Source: Bloomberg. As of August 28, 2026. Source: Nasdaq Data Link . As of August 28, 2026. Includes semiconductors, semiconductor equipment and materials, and diversified and regional banks. Dollar volumes shown in “current day” dollars, deflated by the change in total U.S.-listed stock market capitalization to facilitate long-horizon comparisons. Following the iShares MSCI U.S. Momentum ETF (MTUM) returning a staggering 42.9% in Q2 2026—its largest quarterly return on record going back to 2013—per Figure 7, it has notably retrenched relative to the iShares MSCI U.S. Quality ETF (QUAL). While still higher by 20% YTD as of August 31 st , with MTUM’s top four names being AI stalwarts and comprising 20% of the ETF’s weight, and semis accounting for over 35% of the ETF’s weight, MTUM has sold off as investors have rotated into other parts of the market. When the quality factor outperforms, it can be a signal that investors are favoring corporate characteristics such as earnings durability, balance sheet strength, and low financial leverage amidst a volatile macro backdrop, Fed policy uncertainties, questions around AI capex, and an elevated financing environment. Figure 7: Momentum has sold off while the quality factor has come more into favor Source: Bloomberg. As of August 28, 2026. Solid corporate fundamentals, but watching for slowing earnings growth expectations Market gyrations are typically important to monitor for investor read throughs. But when investing for the longer-term, corporate fundamentals tend to be the driver of equity returns and broader risk taking. Following the outsized, AI-driven S&P 500 earnings growth in Q2, EPS growth is expected to remain very strong over the next three quarters—even if moderating from lofty levels (Figure 8). Likewise, S&P 500 sales growth is expected to be at least 10% YoY through Q1 2027. However, as the base effect becomes more challenging heading into mid-2027, these growth expectations bear watching in terms of a more material slowdown—albeit from very elevated levels. Another key proxy for the health of U.S. corporate fundamentals are credit spreads. The strong corporate earnings dynamics are also expressed via fixed income markets with both high yield and investment grade credit spreads hovering near their tightest levels since mid-2007 (Figure 9). It is worth noting that tech issuance is making up greater portions of the credit market—40% of 15-year-plus investment grade issuance in 2026 has come from companies related to the AI buildout, per Goldman Sachs. Across the pond, the hyperscalers alone comprised over 5% of Euro-denominated IG issuance YTD, per the ECB. On top of the angst around higher rates and AI capex questions, September tends to be the weakest month for U.S. equities historically with an average return of -0.2% since 1945 (Figure 10). The higher rates dynamic coupled with the historical volatility ahead of November U.S. mid-term elections (per our prior report ), could keep market sentiment fragile in the very near-term. title: Second-Quarter Earnings Show Breadth
author: Phil Mackintosh
description: 2026's market rally isn't just AI. Q2 earnings growth hit multi-year highs across chips, large caps, and beyond — with P/E multiples actually falling.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways AI Trade Rotation: From hyperscalers to chipmakers in the "picks-and-shovels" trade. SOX™ Fundamentals-Driven Rally: ~60% YTD price gain matched by ~60% earnings growth; 75% more projected next year. Nasdaq-100® Earnings Breadth at 4½-Year High: Over half of constituents with 20%+ growth; Q2 earnings near 80% p.a. — strongest since 2010. Large-Cap Valuations Compressing: Forward earnings outpacing price returns; P/E multiples falling despite record highs. Broader Than AI: Mid/small caps pricing in recovery on rate cuts, cooling wages, and tax tailwinds — strength extends well beyond chips. For markets, the artificial intelligence (AI) trade has been the dominant theme for the last couple of years. But it has shifted this year. Last year's story was about the AI hyperscalers – the handful of mega-cap tech companies spending hundreds of billions to build out AI infrastructure. This year, investors have rotated one step back in the supply chain. The "picks-and-shovels" trade is here, and chipmakers are the biggest beneficiaries. One constant, though, is that there’s been strong earnings growth underpinning this AI trade all along. In fact, the earnings strength we’ve seen in the AI hyperscalers and now chipmakers is accompanied by a broad-based strength across U.S. equities this year and in second-quarter earnings. SOX semis index sees price return and earnings moving in lockstep A key measure of chips stocks is the PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index™ (SOX™), and it’s up about 60% year-to-date. That's a remarkable number. But what's more remarkable is what's behind it. SOX™ earnings are up over 60% this year (in just two quarters) – roughly in line with the price gain. And analysts project another 75% earnings growth by the end of next year. So, it’s been fundamentals driving this rally. Chart 1: Chips stocks’ prices and earnings are both up about 60% this year That’s also the key difference from the dot-com bubble. In 1999, valuations were running well ahead of earnings (if there were any earnings). Now, earnings are supporting price gains. In fact, for many sectors this year (including the SOX™), price-to-earnings (P/E) multiples are actually falling as earnings rise faster than stock prices (Chart 3). Nasdaq-100® earnings breadth is at 4½-year high The attention on the chipmaker rally can obscure something worth highlighting — earnings growth in 2026 has become remarkably broad-based. As of the second quarter, over half of all Nasdaq-100® companies reported earnings growth of at least 20% per annum (p.a.). More than four in five reported positive earnings growth. Both are the highest readings since the fourth quarter of 2021 — going back to the early post-Covid recovery. This breadth has helped push Nasdaq-100® earnings growth near 80% p.a. in the second quarter — its strongest earnings growth since 2010, when companies were recovering from the depths of the global financial crisis. Chart 2: Earnings breadth pushing Nasdaq-100® near 80% p.a. earnings growth Of course, there are some special circumstances here, with earnings boosted by tariff refunds and marking to market holdings in private companies like Anthropic. Still, even without these factors, large-cap earnings are robust. For large caps, earnings are outpacing returns With the SOX™, the Nasdaq-100® and the S&P 500 all near record highs, it's natural to wonder whether valuations are getting stretched. The data says no — in fact, they’re compressing. Across the major large-cap indexes, forward earnings growth has been outpacing price returns year-to-date. That means P/E multiples are falling as earnings climb faster than prices. That's true for the hyperscalers, the chipmakers, and the broader Nasdaq-100® and S&P 500. Chart 3: Large-cap earnings outpacing price growth, compressing PEs For mid and small caps, markets are betting on stronger earnings The valuation story is a little different once you move down the market cap spectrum. For mid caps (S&P 400), P/E multiples are flat year-to-date. For small caps (S&P 600), they're up nearly 5%. In other words, prices have been rising in line with or a bit faster than earnings for these groups – at most, a modest degree of multiple expansion. Multiple expansion, when it's modest, often reflects investors pricing in expected earnings improvement rather than paying for growth that has already arrived. And there are good reasons to expect it. Earlier rate cuts are feeding through to smaller companies, which carry more floating-rate debt than their large-cap peers. Wage growth is cooling. Tax tailwinds are flowing through to corporate earnings. Market’s strength goes well beyond chips and AI So, what do we make of all this? The SOX™ is the latest headline act and the earnings behind it are real. But framing 2026 as purely a chips or AI story misses most of the picture. The broader market resilience reflects macro tailwinds doing serious work. That combination has lifted a far wider set of companies than the headlines suggest.

title: Protecting Boardroom Trust in an Era of Emerging Cyber Threats
author: Lou Modano
description: Credential abuse appears in 39% of breaches. Identity is the new front line of cyber resilience — and multi-factor authentication (MFA) is the baseline, not the ceiling. Nasdaq CISO Lou Modano breaks down why boards need to move identity security from a checkbox to a core strategy, and what it takes to stay ahead of attackers who increasingly target credentials over systems.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways AI is making phishing, executive impersonation, deepfakes, and credential-harvesting attacks more convincing and scalable Strong access controls for digital governance tools are fundamental to boardroom trust MFA reduces risks from compromised credentials and common identity-based attack paths Boards have always been responsible for protecting sensitive information. Now, they are equally responsible for protecting the identities that have access to it. As organizations rely more heavily on digital platforms to support board communications, decision-making, and governance processes, identity security has become a critical component of cyber resilience. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are making phishing campaigns, executive impersonation schemes, deepfakes, and credential-harvesting attacks more convincing, accessible, and scalable than ever before. While the technology behind these threats continues to evolve, the objective often remains the same: gaining access to sensitive information by compromising trusted identities, credentials, and accounts. Credential abuse was present in 39% of breaches , underscoring the importance of identity security as a foundational element of organizational resilience. Boards are paying attention to these evolving risks. Findings from Nasdaq's 3rd Annual Global Governance Pulse survey suggest cybersecurity and data privacy remain key governance priorities. Among respondents, 35% identified cybersecurity and data privacy as a priority area for continuing education, while 28% said cybersecurity and data privacy expertise would most enhance board composition and 23% identified them as areas likely to affect their organizations over the next 12 months. For boards and governance leaders, the implications are significant. As organizations increasingly rely on digital tools to support governance processes, protecting access to those systems has become a fundamental component of protecting boardroom trust. Strengthening Resilience in a New Era of Cyber Risk Organizations are strengthening resilience through a combination of governance, technology, and security controls. As identity-based attacks become more sophisticated, many organizations are adopting an identity-first approach to security. In an environment where attackers increasingly seek to exploit legitimate access rather than systems alone, resilience depends on understanding who has access to sensitive information, how that access is managed, and how organizations can reduce opportunities for unauthorized use. Responding to these threats requires more than a single security control. Organizations are adopting layered security approaches that combine technology, monitoring, policies, education, and strong access controls. Identity security has become a foundational element of those strategies, helping organizations protect access to critical systems and sensitive information. Identity-First Security in Practice Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is one example of how organizations are strengthening identity security within that broader defense strategy. As identity-based attacks continue to grow, organizations that rely solely on passwords face increasing risk. By requiring an additional form of identity verification beyond a password, MFA helps reduce risks associated with compromised credentials and unauthorized access. MFA can help mitigate common attack paths, including password reuse following third-party data breaches, credential harvesting through phishing campaigns, account takeover attempts, and unauthorized access resulting from stolen credentials. Given the continued prevalence of these attacks, organizations should prioritize ensuring MFA is consistently deployed across systems used to access sensitive information and address any gaps that may remain. The value of MFA is increasingly measurable. Even when attackers possess valid usernames and passwords, MFA can block unauthorized access in more than 99% of cases . Organizations are taking notice, with 85% reporting a security-first approach to identity, reflecting the growing recognition that protecting identities is fundamental to protecting information. For boards and governance teams, these controls are particularly important. Protecting access to board materials and confidential discussions helps support the trust, accountability, and effective decision-making that modern governance requires. How Nasdaq Is Investing in the Future of Digital Governance As cyber risks continue to evolve, Nasdaq continues to invest in measures designed to help protect sensitive board communications and governance information. Nasdaq maintains a defense-in-depth security program supported by identity and access controls, monitoring, vulnerability management, threat intelligence, and ongoing security investments. These efforts are designed to help organizations address evolving identity-based threats while maintaining an effective and seamless user experience. At Nasdaq, trust is central to how we think about the future of governance. As organizations increasingly rely on digital platforms such as Nasdaq Boardvantage® to support board communications, collaboration, and decision-making, protecting sensitive information remains a priority. Security, usability, and accessibility are interconnected components of a trusted governance framework. The benefits of a layered approach to governance security are increasingly measurable. According to the 2025 Forrester Consulting commissioned study, The Total Economic Impact™ of Nasdaq Boardvantage, advanced security capabilities including single sign-on, MFA, encryption, and audit trails reduced the likelihood of a data breach by 40% , representing an estimated $132,000 in avoided breach-related costs over three years. 1 Ultimately, the goal extends beyond reducing risk. It is about enabling boards and leadership teams to make informed decisions with confidence, knowing the systems and processes that support governance are designed to help protect what matters most: trust. Footnote: 1 This information pulled from the Forrester Consulting case study commissioned by Nasdaq as of September 2025 titled, “The Total Economic Impact™ of Nasdaq Boardvantage,” which reflect a composite organization representative of the interviewed decision-makers.

title: How Nasdaq is Turning Tokenized Collateral into Operating Reality on the Canton Network with Vanguard and Wellington Management
author: Roland Chai
description: Read more about test trades led by two of the world's leading asset managers that demonstrated the benefits of tokenization, collateral mobility and operational feasibility.
content: The collateral management challenge facing financial institutions is well understood. Aging infrastructure platforms built for a different era — characterized by fragmentation, manual processes, and high frictional costs — continue to constrain the movement of capital in ways that impose real costs on firms every day. Nasdaq research puts a number on it: 25% of collateral is currently tied up in corrective and non-interest-bearing measures, with the average tier 1 bank holding over $35 billion in idle capital. This represents an extraordinary amount of capital that could be redeployed, risk that could be reduced, and operational complexity that could be eliminated. Tokenizing collateral and the use of distributed ledger technology are a significant unlock for the industry, but market leaders have needed clear proof that tokenized collateral can operate within the same institutional workflows and with the same confidence that markets demand. Nasdaq has now taken another important step toward making that a reality. I am pleased to share that two of the world’s leading asset managers, Vanguard and Wellington Management, have successfully completed their first tokenized collateral trades on the Canton Network. The test trades demonstrated how Nasdaq Calypso can connect, post, and accept tokenized assets as eligible collateral alongside existing pools. The entire workflow, from eligibility determination and margin call generation through to on-chain transfer and post-trade reconciliation, operated within Calypso's existing front-to-back environment, with no manual intervention required at the point of settlement. Crucially, it was conducted within existing operational frameworks, with the same security and integrity that institutional markets require, and at the scale that makes it meaningful. title: LBMA Precious Metals market volumes, June-August 2026, and their significance
author: StoneX
description: Early easing, consolidation then a n August recovery.  Hormuz and bonds (naturally intertwined) the key driver; bond markets treat intervention with some disdain
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Precious metals experienced three distinct phases during June-August 2026: early weakness, summer consolidation, and a strong recovery in August. Silver remained the strongest performer, gaining approximately 159% over the previous year. ETF holdings increased and speculative long positions expanded significantly during August, reflecting renewed investor confidence. Options volumes nearly doubled compared to the same period in 2025, highlighting increased hedging and speculative activity. The LBMA precious metals market between June and August 2026 was defined by a transition from correction to recovery. Early easing, consolidation then a n August recovery. Hormuz and bonds (naturally intertwined) the key driver; bond markets treat intervention with some disdain Rhona O’Connell, StoneX Financial Ltd; 4 th September May 2026 Any views expressed here are of the writer and do not reflect a house view from NASDAQ. Welcome to our monthly round-up of the LBMA OTC trading volumes in gold, silver, platinum and palladium, as recorded on a daily basis by the Association. These are split into spot, swap/forward, options and LoanLeaseDeposit (LLD) and give a flavour of the markets’ activity and how they were influenced by external forces and news items.   Due to technical issues plus some holiday leave, this piece looks back at the June-August this year against June-August 2025 All references to COMEX or NYMEX positioning refer to Managed Money, not commercial positions. General introduction: Daily June-August average compared with daily average for the equivalent period in 2025. Source: LBMA Source: LBMA, StoneX Colour coding ranks the metals against each other in each sector June to August was a particularly eventful period for the precious complex, with the intersection of a hawkish new Fed, an interventionist Treasury, a re-escalating Gulf war, and a structurally weak dollar. Gold, silver, platinum and palladium, September 2025 to early September 2026 Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Silver still the outperformer at +159%; Platinum 125%, Gold 124% and palladium, 118% The three key drivers overall included the vicissitudes of the Gulf war, a dollar that was weak against the euro while strong against the yen – although it could be argued that the yen was independently weak - and a virtual tug-of-war developed between Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessen, which is particularly relevant for gold. By the end of the period, the dollar-debasement argument, which had been fading, reasserted itself. After the rally in May, especially in silver, all four metals drifted lower through June and July as the summer doldrums set in and once again some major players were unwilling to take strategic positions.  The dollar strengthened in June during the ceasefire in the Gulf but once escalation had resumed the currency entered a downward path that only paused for breath in late August. The metals did rally in late June as the Gulf ceasefire failed, with reciprocal strikes between the US and Iran raising new doubts over the return of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.  As we write in early September those doubts have still not been dispelled. In the background it was interesting to see the rising correlation between Brent and the US 10Y yield, but not that surprising since they are both rooted around the Gulf conflict and by definition gold forms part of this matrix also. Growing correlation between Brent and the US 10Y yield since the onset of hostilities Source: Bloomberg, StoneX January 2025 – early September2026 spot volumes, tonnes Gold Silver Source: for all charts above; LBMA, StoneX Platinum Palladium COMEX, NYMEX, positioning to 25 th August 2026 GOLD SILVER PLATINUM PALLADIUM Source: CFTC, StoneX Gold Gold sold off hard in June then spent July trading around $4,100 and occasionally dipping toward $4,000 in one interesting development, gold opened lower on July 13 and fell further despite the US–Iran airstrikes over that weekend, a telling sign that the hawkish-Fed/yield story was overriding the geopolitical safe-haven bid at that point. From a mid-July trough just below$4,000, the metal then staged its best stretch of the year, rallying: by 18% from its mid-July low to an intraday high of $4,696 on August 25 th , its highest since mid-May, before snapping a five-day winning streak late in the month after US inflation data came in above target, then steadying near $4,400–$4,600 into month-end. That mid-August week was gold's best since January, and gold-mining stocks had their hottest five-day run since 2008. Inverted gold and the real two-year yield Source: Bloomberg, StoneX It may seem counter-intuitive that gold prices were rising in the face of continuing increases in bond yields, but this is explained as follows.  Yields were rising on inflation and fiscal fears  rather than growth; a widening fiscal deficit, inflation persistently above 2% (for 65 months above target as Keviin Warsh noted in his Jackson Hole presentation at end-August), a weaker dollar, and an avalanche of corporate bond issuance to fund AI and data-centre build-outs — which is precisely an environment in which gold can flourish. Second, and probably more significantly, the Treasury Secretary’s efforts to suppress yields via FX intervention (something which almost invariably fails) were seen by the markets as an effort at fiscal dominance and financial repression: an admission that the debt load could no longer tolerate market-clearing rates. Sure enough, by early September 30-year yields were back over 5.2%. The US 5Y-30Y curve; long-term Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Adding to gold’s August rally were soft inflation numbers, but not soft enough for the Fed and Mr Warsh’s Jackson Hole comments were visibly more hawkish than the post-FOMC Press conferences held previously. Trading activity Turnover, M ounces Source: NASDAQ, LBMA As far as market turnover is concerned, the sell-off in early June was in the heaviest volume of the period, with over 30M ounces traded on each of three consecutive days.  The rest of June was relatively busy but turnover in July was paltry.  After some improvement in early August, the 5 th was particularly heavy as optimism grew over the possibility of Hormuz being reopened and with hedge funds getting on board gold rallied from $4,066 to $4,268, laying the foundations for consolidation in a new range, and latterly for the rally to almost $4,700 at month-end.  That rally was in relatively thin conditions until the high-volume sell-off on the 28 th in the wake of Kevin Warsh’s comments. Gold from September 2025 Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Among the OTC derivative sectors, swaps/forwards were sluggish in June until towards month-end when, after falling below the 10-day moving average, forward activity picked up and helped to drive the price to the low for the period ($3,943 intraday). Activity increased in July and on more than one occasion seemed to be related to technical indicators, notably the moving averages. This was mirrored to an extent in the LLD segment, notably in early mid-July where heavy activity around $4,100 suggests that there was some supply-side hedging going through the market as prices failed at this level.  As LLD volumes drifted off, the path higher became easier and indeed there was only one LLD trading day in August and that came on the 5th, quelling an initial attempt to clear $4,400. Volumes were high in mid-late July, with prices moving sideways, suggesting good two-way activity.  After a busy day early in August, with a failed assault on $4,400, swaps/forwards tailed off. Finally the options market the volume over the period was almost double that of June-August 2025, with a daily average of almost 1.1M ounces. Even so, volumes were sluggish in June and July.  The stand-out day, with 4.9M ounces going through was again 5 th August, along with high volumes in spot and swaps/forwards, suggesting that part of that swollen volume was hedging against options exposure.  This was on that same day when the market rallied off the 20-day moving average at $4065 to $4,268; i.e. the 5 th when on hopes that Hormuz would reopen. Over the period the ETF gold holdings opened at 4,121t, briefly continued the decline that had started in mid-May, but then turned higher to close Augst at 4,181t, a net year-to-date gain of 156t.  CFTC figures show outright Managed money longs rising from 402t to 497t on 25 th August, while outright shorts fluctuated from 54t to 64t the following week, fluctuated around 50t for much of the rest of the period before short covering into 23t in early Augst ; they closed the period higher again, at 47t. Gold and the S&P (log-scales) Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Silver As usual, silver was the highest-beta play on the same macro forces outlined above, and once again it moved violently. After a January record near $121–$122, it had already halved by early summer, opening June at $74 before a two-leg tumble to $56 on the 24 th , and entering a five-week period in a sideways trend between$55 and $63. This set the scene for the August recovery, with silver reaching an intraday high of &1 on the 28 th before, with gold, going into reverse post-Warsh. Gold and silver action, correlation Source: Bloomberg As well as the major factors that drove gold and by association, silver, the latter metal also has its industrial character to address, given that 70% of silver fabrication (ex-investment) is in industrial uses.  The June-quarter hawkish Fed hold at 3.50–3.75% and a divided committee hit silver's industrial engine directly, and the gold-silver ratio widened from a May low near 55:1 to about 69:1 by mid-July — a classic sign of silver underperforming gold in a risk-off environment. The same soft-data/weak-dollar cocktail that lifted gold then drove the August rebound, amplified by silver's leverage.  The August rally was accompanied, and to some extent driven by, the return of Managed Monay longs (after quite an exodus earlier in the year), rising from 2,822t in mid-July to 3,444t in late August, while shorts were slower to respond, having continued to expand to 1,368t in  mid-August (from 941t in mid-July) then contracting to 1,143t in late August. Gold:silver ratio Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Although the US economy is relatively resilient and the onset of AI, vehicle electrification and solar cells will combine to take silver into an expanding pre-investment deficit, in the immediate term these forces are muffled to a degree with the current surplus of solar cells (and a minor threat from copper) while the ebbs and flows of vehicle electrification are a matter of record – although this is more relevant to the PGM than to silver; see below. Turnover Source:  NASDAQ Spot volumes were down 39% over the period compared with June-August 2025.  With the exception of 5 th August, much mentioned in our gold comments (Hormuz hopes), silver’s spot volume fluctuations were similar to those of gold with high volume in the June retreat (thus making the market less crowded) and then a sluggish period through to mid-July. As prices stabilised spot activity cautiously increased, although volumes in the rally to $70, which was reached on 21 st August, were patchy.  On the 21 st , volumes were much livelier. As hedging activity developed (increased volumes in swaps/forwards and options also) and called a halt to the rally.  After three successive efforts to clear $70, the market capitulated and the sharp fall to $66 on the 28 th was in heavy spot volume (but not in the derivatives). Derivatives activity was heavy in June in swaps and forwards, which will certainly have been instrumental in the price fall and would to some extent have been self-fulfilling.  The LLD segment was 25% down on the 2025 equivalent and here, too , was busiest in the June fall.  There was some cautious interest in mid-August when silver was flirting with $65, suggesting some hedging, especially as the price didn’t clear that level at that stage.  Finally there was activity at month-end as silver was again on the retreat. Platinum and palladium Platinum was the "cleanest" fundamental story of the four, driven more by physical scarcity than by the dollar. The market is expected to be in deficit for the fourth consecutive year this year, despite expected falls in auto and jewellery demand, while supply is likely to be broadly steady.  South Africa accounts for roughly 72% of refined production, and that concentration was the summer's active risk. National primary output fell from about 5.3 million ounces in 2006 to roughly 3.9 million in 2025 and while looking steady this year it is expected to decline again next year. On the demand side, the hydrogen fuel-cell demand, while coming from a very low base, adds a new industrial floor. Palladium trades heavily on autos (80% of demand comes from catalytic converters in gasoline and hybrid vehicles) so it is exposed to two secular headwinds; platinum substitution and the rise of battery-electric vehicles. The June price softness reflected slower automaker procurement, soft electronics demand, caution in the jewellery sector, plus almost non-existent investment, while supply was steady. The July bounce was seasonal restocking rather than scarcity.  The one genuine supply-side tail risk remains geopolitical — Russia is the world's largest palladium producer (nickel by-product), followed by South Africa (platinum by-product) so any escalation of sanctions on Russian metal would be the scenario that could override the surplus narrative, much as it did in 2022.  This is still up in the air. Turnover Source: NASDAQ Platinum spot turnover was 49% down on the equivalent period of 2025, while options and LLD were both down by ~20%.  Swaps/forwards were the only sector in the black, up by 21%.  Trading volumes were choppy, with a couple of heavy days trading in spot in the first week as prices came extended a slide from $1,980 ,although this was not mirrored in the OTC derivatives. The sharp fall from $1,906 to $1,772 was one of those days, and Spot volumes dwindled thereafter as prices slid to $1,535 on 1st July. At this point spot and forwards kicked in, in a classic surge in volume in a price reversal and   suggesting industrial forward buying, sparking a period of price consolidation, during which the only point of interest was heavy forward activity on the approach to $1,700, which failed, implying continued industrial interest and quite possibly inventory management. Early August saw heavy volumes in spot forwards and options as prices surged from $1,629 to$1,751, stemming from a second day of oil price declines and a weaker dollar (Gulf again), taking all the metals higher and precipitating a change of range.  After a period of consolidation the rally to a four-time failed test of $1,900 enjoyed good volumes in everything except options and the reversal saw strong spot activity, suggesting profit taking / stale bull liquidation. Platinum, palladium and the ratio, five-year view Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Palladium prices moved closely in line with platinum over the period, with the correlation between the two not dropping below 0.84, and reaching 0.90 on occasion. Spot trading patterns were not that similar, however, with the early June fall being more of a thin volume slide. There was some intermittent interest in late July in both spot and forwards as the market started to benefit from its prior period of price consolidation, and setting the scene for the sharp jump in early August that had affected all four metals.  Forwards were busy in late July on the approach to $1,300, while there was little options activity until mid-August as prices completed a bear move from the failure at $1,400.   That failure had itself been accompanied by heavy LLD volume, suggesting some hedging activity. title: Slicing the ETF Market 9 Different Ways
author: Phil Mackintosh
description: See how the U.S. ETF market breaks down by total assets, value traded, and product count — revealing where passive, active and levered ETFs lead.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Three New Lenses: ETF market share sliced by total assets, value traded, and product count — each telling a different story. U.S. Stocks Dominate Assets: Sizable international and fixed income exposures; commodities and crypto punch above their weight in trading. Not All Passive: Passive holds 87% of assets and 92% of liquidity, but active funds make up 49% of ETPs and ~47% of 2026 inflows. Levered ETFs Trade Hot: Just a sliver of assets, yet 13.4% of daily value traded and 44.5% of share volume — used as trading vehicles, not buy-and-hold. Exposure Over Size: Passive giants dominate the core, but crypto, active, and levered products lead at the edges. Earlier this summer, we included a chart in our intern’s guide to exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that showed how ETF liquidity can be broken down. It highlighted the diversity of exposures now available in the ETF wrapper, from stocks and bonds to passive and active, as well as different portfolio leverage. Chart 1: ETF liquidity can be measured in many ways Today, we break that data down into three more ways. Instead of looking at share volumes, we look at market share by total assets, value traded and by the number of ETFs in each category. Each tells a different story about what investors and traders like about ETFs. Looking at ETF exposure by asset class One of the great things about ETFs is that they let investors use stock markets to invest in far more than stocks. The chart below looks at asset allocation across the three new metrics. Chart 2: U.S. ETF exposures by asset class – North American exposure dominates The majority of assets in U.S. ETFs hold U.S. stocks. However, there are sizable exposures to international stocks and fixed income. Drilling into liquidity, we see relatively more trading in commodities (gold) and cryptocurrencies (teal). Interestingly, the number of products is more evenly spread across all categories, highlighting an incredible amount of choice across all categories. Specifically, there are a large number of alternatives ETFs, which includes the ETFs with options and target date funds. Not all ETFs are index products It’s a common myth that ETFs are all index funds. This data proves that’s not (entirely) true. Chart 3: Passive ETPs win on total assets, but active strategies trade 10% of daily volumes To be fair, passive management still dominates assets and liquidity, with 87% of assets and 92% of liquidity. Things change at the fund count level. Active funds are 49% of all ETPs by count. Interestingly, ETFGI reports that active ETFs account for nearly half (47%) of fund inflows in 2026, with $529.96 billion in year-to-date net inflows. Looking at ETF leverage ETFs and futures could both be called “derivatives” as they represent a ticker that gets you exposure to something else. Futures have always been levered, with expiry rolls, margin and potential margin calls all part of managing a futures position. The recent evolution of “Perps” has created similar leverage for investors. Some ETFs also provide leverage (although by rule, U.S. leverage has been capped at a much lower 2-times, typically). Chart 4: Unlevered ETFs dominate assets and issuance, and are the majority of trading Despite representing a fraction of assets, levered ETFs account for roughly 13.4% of daily value traded. Mathematically, that shows they are being used as trading vehicles and not held as long as other ETFs. Interestingly, levered ETFs account for a much higher 44.5% of daily share volume. That’s because many levered ETFs have low stock prices – making their share volumes higher for the same value traded. So, what does this tell us? For much of the ETF market, the giant passive index trackers do have outsized share. But at the edges, the divergences are sharp. Levered products, crypto ETFs and active strategies each punch well above their weight in certain categories. The question might not be how big the ETF market is — but which type of exposure you actually want to buy.

title: Biweekly Investment Insights: Markets swirl
author: Yanni Angelakos
description: The Federal Reserve raising rates by 25 basis points and signaling at least one more hike by the end of 2026 as inflation pressures persist. Treasury 10-year yields closing above 5% for the first time since mid-2007. Oil back over $100. Calls for AI deployment to be reined in. U.S. equities in the weakest seasonal period (per Bank of America, the average S&P 500 return during September-October is -0.56% since 1928). There is no shortage of cautious signals for equities and risk assets in the interim.
content: Yanni Angelakos, Head of Investment Insights, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms Mike Cho, CFA, Senior Research Analyst, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms Tony Kristic, Senior Research Analyst, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Equities recalibrate amidst higher Treasury yields August inflation dynamics cemented the Fed raising rates by 25 basis points on September 16 Higher Treasury yields & calls for an AI industry-wide slowdown have pressured equities Earnings growth continues to be the focal point for equity returns as multiple expansion is pressured The Federal Reserve raising rates by 25 basis points and signaling at least one more hike by the end of 2026 as inflation persists. Treasury 10-year yields closing above 5% for the first time since mid-2007. Oil back over $100. Calls for AI deployment to be reined in. U.S. equities in the weakest seasonal period (per Bank of America, the average S&P 500 return during September-October is -0.56% since 1928). There is no shortage of cautious signals for equities and risk assets in the interim. Drawdowns are frequent during the course of the year—broader U.S. equities have averaged more than three pullbacks of 5%+ a year since 1930 (per Bank of America)—but there has only been one in 2026 (March). Per our Biweekly Chart in Focus, Treasury 10-year yields sustaining above 4.50% have tended to pressure Nasdaq-100® forward valuations over the past three years. That is why we suspect that it is unlikely that future equity appreciation will be driven by multiple expansion—instead, it will be about earnings growth which has driven total equity returns over the past year. While the aforementioned headwinds are likely to keep markets under pressure in the near-term given ongoing derisking, equity returns have broadened amidst wider, supportive earnings trends which continues to expand the opportunity set for investors. Biweekly Charts in Focus: Sustained Treasury 10-year yields >4.50% have been a headwind for equity valuations the past 3 years Source: Bloomberg. As of September 14, 2026. Details Latest inflation data cements Fed’s 25 basis point hike The Fed raised rates as expected on September 16 th by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, while the median FOMC projection is forecasting one more rate increase by year’s end. Although the median FOMC projection is not calling for additional rate hikes next year, eight policymakers supported raising by an additional 25 basis points by the end of 2027. For historical context, while the beginning and end dates of official Fed cycles can be debated, per Bloomberg, there have only been two single-hike Fed cycles since 1970 (June 1975 and March 1997). Similar to the June 2026 meeting, 18 out of 19 officials provided rate projections for 2026 and 2027, with Fed Chair Warsh the lone abstainer from submitting forecasts (as in June)—in-line with his public pushback on forward guidance. With the Fed raising rates and its hawkish tilt, it has likely gained credibility with the bond markets as it demonstrates that it is following through on its willingness to attempt to tackle inflation—which could help to keep a lid on Treasury yields relative to it not acting. Elsewhere, major central banks are also on the move to combat inflationary pressures: the ECB raised rates by 25 basis points on September 10 th , as expected, citing persistent inflation above target and the markets are pricing in a full 25 basis point hike by the BoJ on September 18 th . Market pricing for a 25 basis point hike at the September 16th FOMC meeting was practically solidified following the latest August inflation reports (Figure 3), against the backdrop of a relatively resilient U.S. economy. First, PPI rose 0.4% MoM—the largest monthly gain since May—and 5.4% YoY, a beat versus the 5.3% expected and a sharp acceleration from July's 4.8%. The headline was driven almost entirely by a 4.2% surge in energy prices, with food prices contributing a modest 0.1% (per Bloomberg). Core PPI, stripping out food and energy, came in at 0.2% MoM—a miss versus the 0.3% consensus. However, markets largely looked past the soft core print: jumps in airfares and hospital services within the PPI details, combined with upward revisions to July's level, neutralized the headline beat and kept the hawkish read intact. Then, the CPI headline matched expectations at 0.4% MoM and 3.4% YoY, unchanged from July. Per Bloomberg, more than a third of the monthly gain came from a 3.9% rebound in gasoline prices, with food up a modest 0.1%. The surprise was in core CPI, which rose 0.3% MoM against a consensus of 0.2%. On a YoY basis, core CPI came in at 2.4%, the slowest since March 2021, but the monthly acceleration was what moved markets. Digging deeper into core CPI components, shelter was a key driver, rising 0.3%—its largest monthly gain in three months—reversing two months of subdued readings and owners' equivalent rent also picked up. Beyond shelter, wireless phone services jumped notably, also contributing to the core beat. Figure 2: Equities weaker on average following the start of prior Fed rate hiking cycles before recovering Source: Goldman Sachs The most closely watched sub-component of the CPI report as it’s the closest proxy to core PCE—the Fed’s actual inflation target—given the lower shelter weight, is supercore CPI (services ex-shelter). This gauge rose 0.51% MoM (per Bloomberg’s proxy)—the fastest pace since January. This measure, which the Fed tends to view as the most persistent and policy-sensitive component of inflation, saw core services exert a broader influence than energy on the month, reinforcing that price pressures are not confined to volatile categories. Treasury 10-year yields closing above the key threshold of 5% for the first time since July 2007 have been driven by the recent inflation reports and, relatedly, the ongoing resurgence in oil prices (Figure 4). WTI crude oil is back over $100 following the latest escalation in attacks in the Iran war and as Saudi Arabia halted its East-West pipeline which was struck by multiple attacks on September 10th. This pipeline has the capacity to carry about 7 million barrels a day to a key hub on the Red Sea (per Bloomberg) and functioned as an integral bypass of the Strait of Hormuz. Figure 3: August CPI & PPI reports maintained the sticky inflation narrative Source: Bloomberg. Figure 4: Moves in Treasury 10- and 30-year yields have been a byproduct of higher oil prices recently Source: Bloomberg. As of September 14, 2026. Valuation headwinds vs. earnings tailwinds Per Baird Strategas and Figure 5, higher inflation regimes since 1950 have tended to coincide with lower trailing U.S. equity valuations. When focusing on this relationship since 2008, equity multiples have tended to expand despite steps-up in inflation. However, this was greatly skewed during the 2021-2023 inflation spike as equity valuations initially expanded as earnings collapsed but prices recovered rapidly due to the historic fiscal and monetary stimulus during Covid-19. As rates and the inflation backdrop pressure equity valuations, it will likely come down to earnings growth to be the predominant driver. Per the refreshed Figure 6, it has been earnings growth which has driven all of U.S. equity total returns on a net basis over the past year, and not multiple expansion. In the interim, elevated valuations can face headwinds without the shelter of earnings season. Figure 5: S&P 500 average trailing P/Es by inflation tranche Source: Baird Strategas. As of June 30, 2026. Figure 6: Equal-weighted equities have rallied strongly vs. cap-weighted since Q4 2025 Source: FactSet. As of September 14, 2026. Notes: residual is allocated to multiple expansion Also likely feeding into the recent market psyche is the concern that increasing calls from AI research and deployment leaders to slow development, in addition to data center moratoriums, could weigh on earnings expectations across the AI ecosystem. The policies and regulations around AI deployment have yet to take hold as U.S. policymakers must weigh instituting AI guardrails against losing ground to China in the AI race. In the interim, this latest AI rhetoric has contributed to the ongoing churn in equity markets which remains top-of-mind for us. Figure 7 shows how AI-linked proxies (e.g., semiconductors, U.S. large cap growth, Nasdaq-100) have underperformed since the prior peak in the Nasdaq-100 on June 2 nd , while value and small cap groups have outperformed. YTD returns for the likes of semiconductors and the Nasdaq-100 remain solid as do the returns for international, U.S. large cap value, and equal-weighted U.S. stocks—speaking to the broader opportunity set. We’d be remiss, though, if we did not flag the recent weakness in U.S. small caps relative to the mega cap tech cohort since the recent lows in Treasury 10-year yields on August 25 th , which immediately preceded Fed Chair Warsh’s Jackson Hole more hawkish speech on August 28 th . Given the greater sensitivity to changes in rates on account of their relatively higher floating rate exposure as a percentage of total debt—around 5.5x higher, per Bloomberg—the Nasdaq U.S. Small Cap TM Index (NQUSS TM ) is -4.4% versus the Nasdaq-100 which is -0.9% since August 25 th (as of September 15 th ). Figure 7: Only U.S. large cap value, small cap & U.S. large cap equal-weighted equities are positive since June 2 nd Nasdaq-100 highs Source: Bloomberg. As of September 14, 2026. As we’ve discussed in prior reports, the broadening of U.S. equity returns is consistent with the broadening of corporate earnings trends. As another example, Figure 8 below per Bank of America Securities’ U.S. equity strategy team speaks to this trend. With more than 80% of S&P 500 stocks growing EPS YoY in Q2 2026, that puts it in the 94th percentile [ZC2.1]of historical readings shown in Figure 8. The strong earnings construct for megacap tech is a clear example of solid corporate fundamentals. A market concern which has grown louder, though, has come as hyperscalers have issued more debt to support their massive capex initiatives.  Net new debt levels have certainly increased which has caused market angst. That said, per Figure 9 below, a sampling of seven AI hyperscalers shows that approximately two-thirds of total capex is being funded by operating cash—which speaks to the high profitability and strong cash flows of these companies. For more details, please see the recent report from our Index Insights team. Figure 8: Improving earnings breadth across S&P 500 companies Source: Bank of America Merrill Lynch Figure 9: Total capex (AI & non-AI) by funding source amongst AI builders Source: Exponential View, Nasdaq Index Insights. Notes: Analysis based on company filings (funding identity: cash = capex – leases – debt); 2026E based on current company guidance. As of 8/10/26. Of the ~$863B in total capex, ~$550B is estimated to be AI-related. Seven AI builders: Alphabet, Amazon, CoreWeave, Meta, Microsoft, Nebius, Oracle. content: Key Takeaways Proxy season now serves as a multi-year tool to assess board governance, demanding early and ongoing preparation. title: Banking on You Featuring Timberland Bank
author: MarketInsite
description: Janice and Warwick Bryant turned a lifelong dream into reality with a loan from Nasdaq-listed Timberland Bank, building Kaukiki Farms, a 150-acre working farm and wildlife conservancy on Washington's Key Peninsula that now stands as a model of community and land stewardship.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Janice Bryant and her husband, Warwick Bryant, turned their dream of farm ownership into reality by purchasing and developing Kaukiki Farms with support from Timberland Bank. The 150-acre farm is built on sustainable practices, producing grass-fed livestock while preserving wildlife habitats and natural resources. A long-standing relationship with Timberland Bank has supported multiple family and business ventures, highlighting the value of personalized community banking. The Bryants have created a lasting legacy by protecting 114 acres of their property through the Great Peninsula Conservancy, ensuring long-term environmental stewardship. Kaukiki Farms demonstrates how responsible farming, community partnerships, and conservation can coexist for future generations Buying the (Dream) Farm: The Story of Kaukiki Farms Janice Bryant was a 4H girl from Iowa. Her husband, Warwick, grew up on a sheep and beef farm in New Zealand. Together, with a property loan from Timberland Bank, they found themselves preserving an idyllic corner of the Pacific Northwest. "We literally bought the farm," said Janice, co-owner of Kaukiki Farms with Warwick. Nestled on 150 acres on Washington's Key Peninsula, Kaukiki was a dream come true for the Bryants: the kind of place that could be mistaken for a film set, where grass-fed Angus cattle and sheep graze while the surrounding forests, streams, and wildlife habitat are carefully conserved. "We'd both grown up on farms and always wanted to have one," said Janice. In 2007, the opportunity "came to us kind of by happenstance." Through a former business, the Bryants had become familiar with, and captivated by, the Kaukiki property. They approached the owner to work out a deal. "We rented for six months, which applied against our balance, agreed on a price, and then we managed to somehow wiggle, niggle, find our ways and get a mortgage." "We said, wow, if we can make this work, what a great way to bring our boys up in an environment like the ones we had, one they could really appreciate. And so that's kind of how it all started. It was trying to replicate our childhoods for our children." A farm built on care The Bryants raise sheep and cattle primarily on grass and hay grown right on the farm. They manage their pastures carefully and take a deliberate approach to the health of both their animals and the land. Nearly two decades later, Kaukiki has become much more than a family farm. It's a community-renowned operation, a source of locally raised food, a wildlife refuge, and a model of land stewardship the Bryants hope will endure long after they're gone. A family banking relationship Shortly after Timberland Bank opened its Gig Harbor, Washington, office, Chief Residential Loan Manager Richard Pifer was introduced to the Bryants through their realtor. Over the years, the relationship has grown into one rooted in family and community, as Timberland assisted the Bryants and their sons with personal and business ventures alike, including their son's newest endeavor, Kiwi Fencing. "My dad gave me a bit of advice a long time ago: you should always know your banker," said Janice. "But you want a bank that is small enough that you really know the people who are there. Timberland has been just that." "When you walk in, they know you. You have a relationship. And so we started that relationship with Timberland, and it's been fabulous over the years." Janice recalls her time as School Board President of the private school both families attended, when the school fell on hard times. "We had to refinance a loan with really no capital. I was able to sit down with Richard at Timberland and say, 'Richard, is there any way we can do something?'" "And he found a way to make it work. It's been great. I wander in with a full stack of checks because I'm running between balancing hay and kids and everything else, and they're always there to make sure it all comes together." A legacy of conservancy Perhaps the most meaningful chapter of this story is the original loan Timberland provided to help the Bryants build their dream home, a property now part of the Great Peninsula Conservancy, with 114 acres of land permanently protected for the benefit of the community. “We actually have water rights, which is rare, and it allows us to irrigate,” said Janice. The quality of Kaukiki's grass is essential to the quality of their beef and lamb products. In fact, the property has a fresh spring fed stream that runs through the middle of the farm. "We have other friends that live in our canyon," said Janice, referring to the wildlife. "They're animals that live on the grass as well, but we love having a spot for them to go. We'll sit at the pond at night with a bottle of wine and watch the bear come out." One of the things the Bryants love most about Kaukiki Farms is how it extends a legacy of farming and conservation to an area that has developed rapidly over the years they've owned it.

title: What's New in Quantum Computing? Nasdaq Explores the Sector's Rise in Innovation and Investment
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: According to McKinsey research, quantum computing could generate multi-billion-dollar enterprise value over the next decade, with an economic impact that could reach approximately $2.7 trillion by 2035.
content: Quantum computing has emerged as a rapidly growing sector. There has been an increase in companies developing the technology entering the public markets in recent years, private investment is accelerating, and Nasdaq Global Indexes has added quantum computing to one of its leading innovation indexes. According to McKinsey research , quantum computing could generate multi-billion-dollar enterprise value over the next decade, with an economic impact that could reach approximately $2.7 trillion by 2035. Quantum computing companies generated just over $1 billion in revenue in 2025 alone. "Quantum technology helps organizations solve problems that are currently costly, difficult, or impractical using classical computers," said Ilaria Sangalli, Head of Index Insights for EMEA at Nasdaq, who authored the index team's research on the quantum sub-theme. Potential applications include molecular simulation for drug discovery, portfolio optimization in finance, supply chain management, and cybersecurity. As emerging technologies require capital to scale, the trend is currently playing out in public markets. Fifteen Nasdaq-listed U.S. companies specializing in AI and quantum computing hardware and software, have a combined market capitalization of about $3.78 trillion. Three-quarters of those companies have listed since 2020, including the recent listings of D-Wave Quantum, Quantinuum, and IQM Quantum Computers, with the largest wave arriving in 2021 and a new cohort emerging in the last two years. [1] The pattern resembles earlier cycles in AI, cloud computing, and cybersecurity, when investors began to treat each as a distinct category. In the recent enhancement of the Nasdaq Global Artificial Intelligence and Big Data™ Index (NYGBIG™), quantum computing became a dedicated sub-theme alongside areas like deep learning, cloud computing, and big data. Since its launch, the index has followed a forward-looking, patent-driven approach designed to identify companies at the forefront of technological innovation. The effectiveness of this approach has been reflected not only in the index's ability to identify innovative companies, but also in its long-term performance. Since its launch on November 12, 2018, NYGBIG has delivered a total return of approximately 384% (22.8% on an annualized basis). This pattern of outperformance has continued throughout the recent AI-driven investment cycle. Since July 2023, NYGBIG generated a total return of 139% (33% on an annualized basis), outperforming the Nasdaq-100®, broader U.S. equities, and several established AI benchmarks. [2] Of the 1,181 companies with patent activity related to NYGBIG's sub-themes, 247 held patents connected to quantum computing. "This suggests that quantum computing is evolving beyond a niche research field into a distinct technology ecosystem," Sangalli said. Her analysis also notes American leadership in the field: U.S. companies account for 58% of the quantum computing contribution score, a measure of each company's share of recently approved patents compared with other companies active in the same field. [3] The research also found that in addition to pure-play companies, the enhancement brought in traditional hardware companies with significant patent activity in the field, which placed them primarily in the quantum computing sub-theme. The quantum sub-theme's inclusion is closely tied to its convergence with AI. Quantum systems could accelerate optimization and simulation tasks running on classical computers, while AI is being applied to quantum algorithm development and error correction. "The two technologies may reinforce one another rather than develop independently," Sangalli said. Investment continues to grow. Quantum technology startups attracted $12.6 billion in venture and private funding in 2025, more than six times the 2024 level, with roughly 90% directed at quantum computing specifically. Governments are engaged, viewing the technology as critical for national security and cryptography; the U.S. government announced about $2 billion in quantum commitments in May 2026 and has taken minority stakes in leading companies. Yet the funding mix has flipped. Public money made up about one-third of total investment in 2024 and just 3% in 2025. Sangalli expects interest in quantum to build as more commercial use cases emerge, with investors gaining exposure through a mix of pure-play quantum companies and larger technology firms investing in the technology through R&D spending, including patent development. The boundaries of the category will likely blur, much as they have elsewhere. "Would you call Microsoft an AI company nowadays?" she said. "It's much more."
